newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airlines lift ex-Paris rates on steady transatlantic demand.
newsitem.headline: Airlines lift ex-Paris rates on steady transatlantic demand.

text.p: PARIS, May 30 (Reuter) Steady demand on transatlantic routes has given several airlines scope to increase rates, a Reuters survey showed.
Paris pacesetter, Air France, raised its rates to Chicago by between 30 and 50 centimes per kg, effective May 15.
"There is a very buoyant demand for non-consolidated, full-load traffic into the U.S. midwest, largely made up of capital goods and equipment," an Air France Cargo official told Reuters.
The French airline increased rates by a similar amounts to New York, Los Angeles and Canada in March, the official said.
"It's unlikely there will be further increases before September and October."
The new full-freighter charter venture launched by Air France between Paris and Atlanta in April has made an encouraging debut, the official added.
"A group of shippers are generating regular traffic in full-load consignments and a longer term aim is to obtain rights for scheduled services on the route."
Of the U.S. belly carriers, United Airlines, raised its ex-Paris rates by seven and half percent, effective May 5.
American Airlines' (AA) plans to up its rates from the same date have been postponed until June 2 as a result of a re-structuring of the carrier's pricing system.
The increases will work out at an average of six percent to U.S. destinations.
AA operates daily passenger services from Paris to New York, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and Dallas.

Commenting on the current state of the market, a Paris-based AA cargo official said: "With all the public holidays in May we feared a bit of a downturn in the strong level of activity we had experienced in the first four months of the year. However, the market has held up rather well with France-originating freight being particularly strong over the past six weeks or so made up of a broad variety of general cargo."

Other Transatlantic belly-carriers, such as Delta Air Lines and Continental, appear to have left rates unchanged leading one industry source to suggest this is probably because they were seeking to pick up business since their recent move from Paris/Orly to Paris/CDG.

Continued market recovery on Paris-U.S. has extended to Canada. "Autumn 1996 marked the turning point on Paris-Canada routes and the recovery has been sustained with belly capacity more or less fully utilised on our services to Montreal and Toronto," said Air Canada's cargo sales and services manager, France and Western Europe, Daniel Bregere.
Air Canada increased its ex-Paris rates to Montreal, Toronto and selected destinations in the U.S. by around five percent from March 1 after a prolonged period of downward pressure on prices.
"Demand is buoyant but we don't see a new round of increases is unlikely to take place before the Autumn."

From the beginning of June, Air Canada will have a daily Boeing 747-400 combi on its Paris-Toronto route compared to 767-200 and 767-300 passenger aircraft during the same peak summer season last year.
Last year, during the same period, Air Canada operated Boeing 767-200 and 767-300 passenger aircraft on the route.

The introduction of the combis on the route will increase our ex-Europe lift significantly on last year and our French cargo station will share capacity with our stations in Germany, Italy and Spain," said Air Canada's cargo sales and services manager, France and Western Europe, Daniel Bregere.

He added: "As far as France-originating freight is concerned, the combis will mean a little more capacity is available on last year and clearly there will be scope to accommodate outsize shipments from our French customers which with the 767s we were hardly in a position to accept," he added.
Air Canada's Paris-Toronto combis, which will operate until end-October, will be backed up with four weekly 767-200 flights on the same route.
The Canadian carrier is also operating a daily Paris-Montreal service, using a 747 passenger aircraft and a three times weekly Paris-Vancouver service using 767-300s.

"Last year, we operated 767-200s on the Paris-Vancouver route and were never really sure of how much freight capacity we could offer because this depended heavily on passenger loads. However, with the 767-300 we can guarantee 10 to 12 tonnes of space on a regular basis which means we can make a serious effort at selling the route."

While Vancouver and the west coast of Canada did not represent a particularly significant market for air cargo from Paris there was the possibility of onward destinations in the U.S. such as Oregon and Washington State.
Air Canada's Paris-Vancouver service begins on June 16 and runs until end-September 1997.
In the LatAm sector, Brazilian carrier, Varig is set to raise cargo capacity significantly next month when it replaces a DC10 with an MD11 on its daily Paris-Sao Paulo-Rio passenger service.
"The change of aircraft will at least double cargo lift on the route, offering between 12 and 14 tonnes per flight," a Paris-based Varig cargo official said.
Varig increased its ex-Paris rates by an average of eight percent from April 1
